chunks.text: Density is a measure of how tightly mass is packed into a given volume of space. An object with tightly packed matter has high density, while an object with spread-out particles has low density.

The formula for density is Density = Mass / Volume (D = M/V). Mass is measured in grams (g) or kilograms (kg), and volume is measured in cubic centimeters (cm³) or milliliters (ml). Density is expressed in g/cm³ or kg/L.
Mass is the total amount of matter inside an object, measured in grams (g) or kilograms (kg). Mass remains constant regardless of gravity or location.

Volume is the amount of three-dimensional space an object occupies, measured in cubic centimeters (cm³) or milliliters (ml). Volume can be measured by multiplying dimensions or by liquid water displacement.

An object floats in water if its average density is less than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³). For example, wood has a density around 0.6 g/cm³, which is less than 1.0 g/cm³, so it floats comfortably on the surface.

An object sinks in water if its average density is greater than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³). For example, iron has a density of 7.8 g/cm³, which is greater than 1.0 g/cm³, so it sinks directly to the bottom.
Ice floats on liquid water because water uniquely expands as it freezes, creating open hexagonal crystal spaces that make solid ice less dense (0.92 g/cm³) than liquid water (1.00 g/cm³).

Giant steel ships float because their hollow hull encloses a vast volume of air. The combined average density of the steel hull plus the enclosed air is significantly less than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³), generating strong buoyant force.

Buoyancy is the upward force exerted by a fluid that opposes the weight of an immersed object. Archimedes principle states that the upward buoyant force is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.

Different liquids form distinct layers based on density. Immiscible liquids will arrange themselves with the most dense at the bottom (like honey at 1.42 g/cm³), water in the middle (1.0 g/cm³), and the least dense on top (like oil at 0.92 g/cm³).

misconceptions.correction: Weight alone does not determine sinking or floating; density does (Mass ÷ Volume). A giant 50,000-ton steel cargo ship floats because its hollow air-filled hull lowers its average density below water, whereas a tiny 2-gram pebble sinks because its density is higher than water.

misconceptions.pattern: big things sink and small things float
misconceptions.correction: Size alone does not determine floating. A massive tree trunk floats because wood is less dense than water (0.6 g/cm³), while a tiny metal pin sinks because metal is denser than water (7.8 g/cm³).
